text: Your class is having a science fair. What do you build?

outcomes.resultText: Your volcano erupted spectacularly during the demonstration -- unfortunately, most of the lava ended up on the judge's table.
Your volcano erupted right on cue. Nothing fancy, but it worked exactly as planned.
Your volcano barely fizzled instead of erupting. A little anticlimactic, but you still got some points for effort.
Somehow your volcano became the highlight of the entire fair. Kids kept coming back just to watch it erupt again.
Your plants under the grow light were noticeably taller than the control group. Clean, convincing results.
Your results were kind of a mess -- some plants under the grow light did worse, not better. You explained the data as best you could.
Most of your plants died a few days before the fair. You presented anyway, mostly on vibes.
You noticed something odd in your data that even your teacher couldn't fully explain. She said it was the most interesting question in the whole fair.
Your solar oven actually melted the s'mores in under ten minutes. The judges were genuinely impressed.
Your solar oven worked, just slower than you'd hoped. You spent most of the fair waiting for chocolate to melt.
It was cloudy on fair day, so your solar oven barely worked. You explained the science anyway, which counted for something.
Your robot flawlessly navigated the obstacle course in front of the judges. You won first place, and the local paper even snapped a photo.
Your robot mostly worked -- it wobbled through the course and only got stuck once. The judges were impressed anyway.
Your robot short-circuited halfway through its demo and started spinning in circles. The crowd loved it more than if it had worked.
Your robot never quite worked right, and you spent most of the demo apologizing to the judges. At least you learned a lot troubleshooting it.
Your science teacher was so impressed she asked you to help her set up the robotics club next year.
Your photo series got its own little corner of the gym, and people kept stopping to look at it.
Your photos were well received, even if they didn't steal the show from the volcanoes.
Half your prints came out blurry because of a camera mishap the night before. You made do with what you had.
You presented your homemade water filter to the judges. The first test didn't go as planned, but you quickly figured out what went wrong and fixed it before the final demonstration.
Your water filter never quite got the water clear enough, and you spent most of your presentation explaining what you'd try differently next time.
Your filter worked better than anyone expected, including you. A judge asked if you'd thought about entering the regional science fair.
Your little wind-and-solar model actually powered a light bulb, and the judges spent a long time asking you how it worked.
Your model mostly worked, though you had to explain away a couple of parts that didn't quite behave as planned.
Your model was too ambitious for the time you had, and it barely worked by the time judging came around.
